TASK: REWRITE THE JOINS

Below is a draft report in six sections. Each section was written separately, so the joins between them are rough. Rewrite the OPENING PARAGRAPH of sections 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 so that each section's opening carries the reader on from the end of the section before it.

RULES
1. Change only the opening paragraphs of sections 2 to 6. Do not touch any other paragraph.
2. Add no fact and drop no fact. Every sentence's markers, written like [c:CL-035], stay exactly as they are, on the sentence that carries that fact; every number stays exactly as written. A rewrite that adds, drops or moves a marker or changes a number is discarded.
3. You may reorder the sentences of an opening paragraph, rephrase them, and add or reword a connective or a short linking clause that states no fact.
4. Keep the register: technical and readable; one thought per paragraph, in its first sentence; known information before new; no em dash or en dash; no fragments after long sentences; none of the words load-bearing, hallucinate, delve, testament.
5. If an opening already joins well, return it unchanged.

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
{"2": ["sentence one of section 2's opening paragraph [c:CL-034].", "sentence two."], "3": [...], "4": [...], "5": [...], "6": [...]}

## 1. What the framework is for

The framework exists to rate and score, quantitatively and qualitatively, whether the public and the tools the public now uses can reach, understand and use the data they paid for [c:CL-085]. The Department of Commerce has set a neighbouring target in its guidance glossary, which defines AI-ready data as data that is not just machine-readable but machine-understandable, enriched with contextual metadata and organized in interpretable standard formats for use by AI systems [c:CL-085]. That glossary belongs to guidance written by the Department's Data Governance Board, not to a Department-wide regulation, and read beside the framework's own statement it describes the data, whereas the framework asks whether people and their tools can get to the data and use it [c:CL-085].

Publishing data and reaching it are separate problems, because each step between a released file and its use can fail on its own [c:CL-078]. Wilkinson and colleagues, setting out the FAIR principles, describe a machine agent that must identify an object, judge it useful, judge it usable with respect to licence, consent and access, and then act, so a machine can complete one step and fail the next [c:CL-078]. Structured metadata on a page therefore does not by itself make data usable by machines, since discovery, access, interpretation and fitness for use are each required [c:CL-078]. Fitness for use is also the term federal statistical guidance uses for data quality, defined there as fitness for a user's own needs [c:CL-078]. For example, figures released in aggregated spreadsheets laid out for presentation are not machine-usable even when published, because a format that machines cannot read places severe limits on what the data can be used for [c:CL-086].

Writing for machine readers already has a named discipline, generative engine optimization, which its originators present as the successor to search engine optimization [c:CL-080]. Those machine readers face a further barrier, because publishers increasingly restrict AI crawlers and the public's access to data through AI tools depends on those restrictions [c:CL-081]. An audit of 14,000 web domains found a rapid rise in such restrictions within a single year, 2023 to 2024 [c:CL-081]. The cost of a restriction falls on the public, since OpenAI states that sites opted out of its search crawler will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, and Anthropic warns that blocking its search crawler may reduce a site's visibility and accuracy in user search results [c:CL-081]. However, no measurement of the AI-crawler policies of U.S. federal sites was found, and the nearest measure, drawn from the robots.txt files of about 140 million sites, reports that 42% of law and government sites blocked AI bots without separating U.S. federal sites from the rest [c:CL-081].

The framework's structure starts from the 4 criteria USAFacts set out, that data be accessible, understandable, accurate and open, and adds 3 more, for 7 criteria in all [c:CL-047]. Below the criteria, the framework record holds 50 indicators, of which 48 are in the framework and 2 are candidates [c:CL-046]. Those 2 candidates, the check for access policy coherence and the check for discoverability from the product page, enter no framework count until the framework's operator adopts them [c:CL-046].

## 2. What was measured, on whom, and how

The measurement behind this report is one composite measurement cycle, scan_2026-10-07_composite_d, which covers 16 statistical bodies [c:CL-050]. Of those bodies, 13 are ranked, because the others have no scored result that rests on a judged finding [c:CL-050]. Across all of them, the cycle judged 24 sets of results and holds 1,055 findings [c:CL-051].

Each of those findings came from a single public client, the scanner, which identified itself by a user agent that names the project and links to its public source [c:CL-034]. Beyond that name the scanner sent nothing, so no credentials, cookies or other identity accompanied any request [c:CL-034]. It also kept the same identity for the whole cycle and never varied it to get a better answer [c:CL-034].

So far, rules measure only part of the framework, because 23 of its 48 indicators have a current rule [c:CL-048]. There are 25 current rules in all, but the rules beyond those 23 indicators belong to the check for access policy coherence and the check for discoverability from the product page, which stay outside the framework count [c:CL-048]. The record's own status marks follow the same line, with 23 of the 48 indicators marked measured, 1 whose measuring tool is built but not yet marked measured, and 24 specified only [c:CL-049].

The framework rests on a corpus of admitted documents that began as a first set of 71 and now holds 282 [c:CL-044]. Of the documents added after that first set, 162 came in before the framework record was first committed and 49 on or after that commit [c:CL-044]. Those 49 later documents are not all literature, however, because 25 of them are captured copies of the scanned web pages rather than published work [c:CL-044].

## 3. What was found: hosts that refused a plain client

Of everything the scanner observed, an access denial is the most direct observation, because it is the host's own answer to a plain, unauthenticated client that identified itself and obeyed robots.txt [c:CL-035, CL-036]. Across all 1,055 findings, 341 are access denials, in which the host returned an HTTP 401, 403 or 429 status, disallowed the request in its robots.txt file, or reset the connection [c:CL-035]. The other findings comprise 415 absences, where the record, field or file is not served, 57 cases where something is served but fails the test applied to it, 65 other errors such as server errors, unparseable responses and a redirect loop, and 177 passes [c:CL-035].

Three statistical bodies account for the most complete refusals. The scanner met a denial on all 45 of its findings for the Bureau of Labor Statistics and on all 45 for the Office of Research, Evaluation, and Statistics at the Social Security Administration, so neither body produced a single absence or a single pass [c:CL-036, CL-041]. The Bureau of Transportation Statistics came close behind, refusing the scanner on 41 of its 45 findings and passing only 2 [c:CL-037]. Bodies with more findings were refused less completely but still often; for example, the Bureau of Economic Analysis denied the scanner on 40 of 89 findings, and the National Agricultural Statistics Service on 36 of 89 [c:CL-087, CL-040].

At the other end of the range, Statistics of Income at the Internal Revenue Service denied the scanner on only 4 of its 67 findings, all of them robots.txt disallows, although 44 of its findings are absences and only 12 pass [c:CL-042]. The National Center for Education Statistics and the National Animal Health Monitoring System each refused 10 of 45 [c:CL-096, CL-095]. Data.gov is a comparator host and not a statistical body, so it is reported apart from them; it refused 1 of its 9 findings and passed 7 [c:CL-043].

These denials say something about public access as well as about the scanner, because the public's access through AI tools depends on the restrictions that publishers place on crawlers [c:CL-081]. OpenAI, for example, states that a site opted out of its search crawler will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers [c:CL-081]. A search of the literature found no earlier measurement of the AI-crawler policies of U.S. federal sites, and the nearest measure, taken across about 140 million websites, reports that law and government sites blocked AI bots more than other categories, with 42% blocked [c:CL-081].

## 4. What was found: what the hosts that answered serve

Where a host did answer, the commonest result was an absence: of the 1,055 findings, 415 are absences, in which the scanner found no record, field or file served, 57 find something served that fails its test, and 177 pass [c:CL-035]. The remaining findings are the 341 access denials already described and 65 other errors, such as server errors, unparseable responses and a redirect loop [c:CL-035]. Absences matter because use by a machine is a chain of steps, in which an agent must discover a product, reach it, interpret it and judge its fitness for use, and a machine that completes one step can still fail at the next [c:CL-078]. Publication does not settle the question either, because tables laid out for presentation must be tidied before analysis, and a format that is not machine-readable places severe limits on what can be done with the data [c:CL-086].

For one publisher, the Census Bureau, the published result tables mark 18 of 39 judged rows as failing [c:CL-052]. Those tables carry one row for each check and page they report, so they hold fewer rows than the 89 findings the scan recorded for the Bureau across every page it probed [c:CL-052]. Every failing row falls on one of the two pages that present the Bureau's flagship programs, its surveys and programs page and its American Community Survey page, and the same checks fail on both [c:CL-052].

The Census Bureau's catalog also shows why a product the scanner did not find must be kept apart from a product that does not exist. The Bureau serves a catalog on its own website holding 1,810 records, but no record in it names the products the scanner probed [c:CL-045]. Federal policy expects such a listing, because each agency must keep a public inventory of all its data assets on its own website, and a flagship product is one of those assets [c:CL-079]. Even so, the 20 Census findings that rest on that catalog, from the checks for variable-level semantics, quality metadata, provenance completeness, no dark data and authority metadata, are recorded as errors rather than failures [c:CL-045]. The reason is that the Commerce Department's inventory, which the check also names, refused the scanner, so although the Bureau's organization on catalog.data.gov was read, absence is not established [c:CL-045]. These findings therefore describe products the scanner could not find in the catalogs it could read, and they do not show that the Bureau left those products unlisted [c:CL-045].

## 5. What the measurement cannot say

A refusal limits what the measurement can say, because a refused request shows only that the scanner was not served, not that the thing it sought is missing [c:CL-045, CL-038]. For the Census Bureau, the scanner, which identified itself and did not log in, met a refusal by the host or a disallow in robots.txt on 24 of the Bureau's 89 findings [c:CL-038]. Among the Bureau's 27 absences, moreover, 4 were judged only after some refused or disallowed probes had been set aside, so those verdicts rest on part of the evidence the checks would otherwise read [c:CL-038]. The limit is sharper still for three bodies, because of the 16 statistical bodies in the cycle only 13 are ranked, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Bureau of Transportation Statistics and the Office of Research, Evaluation, and Statistics have no scored check with a judged row [c:CL-050]. Their absence from the ranking therefore records that no check could be judged on them, and it says nothing about the quality of their products [c:CL-050].

A rank can also rest on far less evidence than a body's full set of findings would suggest [c:CL-052, CL-053]. On the published matrices the Census Bureau has 18 failing of 39 judged rows, and those matrices carry fewer rows than the 89 findings the cycle holds for the Bureau, because they publish one row per check and surface [c:CL-052]. Under the hierarchical equal-weight score, however, the Bureau ranks 7 of 13 with a score of 0.143, and that rank turns on a single check, the check for a definitions surface, on which 0 of 2 judged rows passed [c:CL-053]. Were that one verdict reversed, the Bureau would rank 1, so a reader should take a rank as a statement about a few checks rather than about a body's readiness as a whole [c:CL-053].

The framework is also larger than the part of it this measurement scored [c:CL-046, CL-049]. Its record holds 50 indicators, of which 48 belong to the framework and 2 are candidates, the check for access policy coherence and the check for discoverability from the product page, and a candidate enters no count until the operator adopts it [c:CL-046]. Of the framework's 48 indicators, the record marks 23 as measured, 1 as having its measurement built but not yet marked measured, and 24 as specified only [c:CL-049]. What holds back the 25 indicators not marked measured differs by kind: 11 have no standard to measure against, 7 need the cooperation of agencies, 6 need open tooling, none is blocked by funding, and 1 is not blocked at all [c:CL-001]. Money, therefore, is not what stands between the specified indicators and a measurement of them [c:CL-001].

Finally, only part of the framework's evidence can be traced to an exact place in a source [c:CL-054]. Of 50 indicator evidence cells, 10 carry a pinpoint locator, and of the 154 links that tie an indicator to its evidence, 34 point at a document with a locator [c:CL-054]. Moreover, 16 indicators have no such link at all, and 84 of the 282 documents admitted to the record are cited by one [c:CL-054]. A reader can therefore confirm that a source stands behind much of the framework, but can find the exact passage behind an indicator in only 10 cases [c:CL-054].

## 6. What an agency can do, and what is measured next

For the Census Bureau, every prescribed action that the claims name falls in the notional hours effort band and carries no cost [c:CL-059, CL-060, CL-066, CL-067, CL-068, CL-069, CL-072, CL-073, CL-074, CL-075, CL-076, CL-077, CL-115, CL-116, CL-117]. Under equal weights, each action can raise the bureau's hierarchical score by at most a stated amount, which is what the score would gain if every failing result on that action's check passed; because no weighting is asserted, each amount is a bound and not a value [c:CL-059, CL-060, CL-066, CL-067, CL-068, CL-069, CL-072, CL-073, CL-074, CL-075, CL-076, CL-077, CL-115, CL-116, CL-117]. The widest of these bounds belongs to a change in how releases are recorded: carrying a revision class on every changelog entry addresses the check for change legibility and can add at most 0.25 [c:CL-115]. The terms under which a machine may reuse a product are fixed by two pairs of actions. The first pair is publishing a machine-readable licence for the product and stating that licence as an identifier rather than as a sentence, which address the check for license clarity with a bound of 0.125 each [c:CL-116, CL-117]. The second pair declares the terms for AI training and AI input in robots.txt, using only the categories and values that the Content Signals Policy defines, and each of these two actions, which serve the check for reuse permissions for AI, can likewise add at most 0.125 [c:CL-059, CL-060].

The remaining actions fix how a product explains its concepts and describes itself to a machine. Publishing the product's concept definitions as schema.org defined terms, giving each linked term a code, a term set and a definition, and linking those terms from the product's variables all address the check for definitions surface, and each is bounded at 0.083 [c:CL-066, CL-067, CL-068]. The same bound of 0.083 applies to naming the term set that each term code belongs to, which serves the check for semantic consistency, and to linking the methodology from the product page, which serves the check for methodology legibility [c:CL-072, CL-069]. Actions on the product page's markup carry a bound of at most 0.036 each: embedding JSON-LD that describes the product, typing the page's existing markup as a Dataset, and making that markup conform to the profile it declares all address the check for structured markup [c:CL-073, CL-074, CL-075]. Publishing a release date for the product and declaring its vintage in the markup, not only in a file header, address the check for timeliness of surface under that same bound [c:CL-076, CL-077].

Tying each measured result to a prescribed fix is not new, because outside-in measurement of an organization's published surface, with a remediation step named for each result, is an existing pattern in tools such as Lighthouse and OpenSSF Scorecard [c:CL-082]. However, in the documentation read for this report, none of those results carries an effort estimate, and that absence is recorded over the sources read rather than established for the literature as a whole [c:CL-082]. What this framework adds, therefore, is a notional effort band for each prescribed action and a bound on how far that action can move the score [c:CL-082, CL-115, CL-116].

What the framework measures next depends on what blocks each indicator still unmeasured. Of the 25 indicators that the record does not mark measured, 11 wait on a standard, 7 on the agency's cooperation, 6 on open tooling, 0 on funding, and 1 is not blocked [c:CL-001]. The next measurements therefore take up indicators that can be measured from outside with public tools and no action by the agency [c:CL-002, CL-012, CL-025, CL-026, CL-028, CL-030]. For example, the check for stable identifiers and the check for regression on vintage transition can both be read from the Wayback CDX server, the check for readiness metrics baseline from AIDRIN, and the check for release authenticity from the SLSA verifier [c:CL-002, CL-026, CL-012, CL-028]. The check for contract stability compares two releases with oasdiff, so it must wait for a second scan [c:CL-025]. The check for classification/vintage identity is also within reach, because a standard already admitted to the record names the artifact it would read, and the only missing piece is a collector that this project would write [c:CL-030]. Each of these indicators is to be measured before the summary is drafted, and none of them requires anything from the agency [c:CL-002, CL-012, CL-025, CL-026, CL-028, CL-030].
